Administering Compliant FMLA Leave and Pay for Growing Employers
Crossing into FMLA territory is a common inflection point for growing companies. Once headcount and location footprint cross certain thresholds, leave administration stops being a judgment call and becomes a federal compliance obligation with real exposure attached to getting it wrong. The FAQs below answer the questions that come up most often for owners and HR leads administering FMLA leave for the first time or tightening up a process that has grown inconsistent.
When does FMLA apply to our company and which employees are eligible
FMLA coverage and individual eligibility are two separate tests, and mixing them up is the single most common mistake employers make here. Employer coverage is a company-wide count: a private-sector employer is covered once it has 50 or more employees for at least 20 workweeks in the current or preceding calendar year, with no location or radius attached (public agencies and public or private elementary and secondary schools are covered regardless of size). Employee eligibility is a separate, narrower test layered on top of that: an employee is eligible for leave only if they have worked for the employer for at least 12 months, logged at least 1,250 hours of service in the 12 months immediately before the leave starts, and work at a location where the employer has 50 or more employees within 75 miles.


This is the threshold check growing employers most often get wrong, not because the rule is unclear but because it is easy to apply the wrong headcount snapshot (counting company-wide headcount instead of the 75-mile radius, or counting the wrong 12-month window for an employee’s tenure). Get the coverage and eligibility determination wrong at the front end, and every downstream decision about leave, pay, and job restoration inherits that error. (U.S. Department of Labor, Fact Sheet #28: The Family and Medical Leave Act)
Does PTO run concurrently with FMLA leave or does it run separately
FMLA leave itself is unpaid, and federal rules allow an employer to require, or an employee to elect, that accrued paid leave (vacation, sick time, PTO) run concurrently with unpaid FMLA leave rather than stacking on top of it. Whether substitution applies, and which paid leave categories qualify for which reasons, depends on how the employer’s own paid leave policy is written and applied consistently across the workforce.


The exposure here is inconsistency, not the substitution rule itself. If one manager lets an employee bank PTO for later use during an FMLA absence while another manager requires concurrent use for an employee with the same type of leave, that inconsistency is exactly the kind of documentation gap that creates legal risk. (U.S. Department of Labor, Fact Sheet #28: The Family and Medical Leave Act)
How do we calculate pay during unpaid FMLA leave
Base FMLA leave provides no federally mandated wage replacement. It is unpaid leave by design, and the employer’s obligation is to protect the job and the leave entitlement, not to continue salary. Where an employee has accrued paid leave and the substitution rules described above apply, pay continues at the normal rate for however much of the leave that paid leave covers; once accrued paid leave is exhausted, the remaining portion of the 12-week entitlement is unpaid unless another benefit (short-term disability, a state paid leave program) independently applies.


Payroll needs a clean, consistent process for coding these transitions correctly, especially when an employee moves from paid leave to unpaid leave and back mid-cycle, because a coding error here shows up as a pay accuracy problem on top of a compliance problem. (U.S. Department of Labor, Fact Sheet #28: The Family and Medical Leave Act)
What are our benefits continuation obligations during FMLA leave
An employer must maintain the employee’s group health plan coverage during FMLA leave under the same terms that would have applied had the employee continued working, including the employer’s usual share of the premium. The employee remains responsible for paying their normal share of the premium, and the employer can recover premiums it paid on the employee’s behalf in certain circumstances if the employee does not return from leave.


This obligation runs independently of whether the leave is paid or unpaid through PTO substitution. Benefits continuation is a separate, parallel requirement, and treating it as automatically resolved just because payroll has stopped is a common gap. (U.S. Department of Labor, Fact Sheet #28A: Employee Protections under the FMLA)
What is the most common way employers miscount the 12-week entitlement
The most common miscount comes from applying the wrong method for measuring the 12-month period against which the 12 weeks are tracked. Employers are permitted to choose among four methods, including the calendar year, a fixed 12-month “leave year,” the 12-month period measured forward from an employee’s first FMLA use, or a rolling 12-month period measured backward from any date leave is used, and the method has to be applied consistently once chosen.


Growing companies frequently run into trouble when different managers or locations informally apply different methods, or when intermittent leave (a few hours here, a partial day there) isn’t tracked cumulatively against the total entitlement, which can result in granting more or less leave than the employee is actually owed. (U.S. Department of Labor, Fact Sheet #28: The Family and Medical Leave Act)
What happens if we do not restore an employee to an equivalent position after FMLA leave
An employee returning from FMLA leave is entitled to be restored to the same position they held before leave, or to an equivalent position with equivalent pay, benefits, and other terms and conditions of employment. Failing to do so, absent a narrow exception, is a violation of the employee’s job restoration rights and can expose the employer to an interference or retaliation claim under the FMLA.


This is where legal exposure escalates quickly for growing companies, because “equivalent” is a specific standard (equivalent pay, shift, benefits, and responsibilities), not “the closest open role we happen to have.” A demotion, a schedule downgrade, or a quiet reassignment to a lesser role after leave is a frequent trigger for FMLA complaints. (U.S. Department of Labor, Fact Sheet #28A: Employee Protections under the FMLA)
How should we document FMLA leave to avoid inconsistent practices that create legal exposure
Consistent documentation means using the same eligibility notice, designation notice, and certification process for every employee requesting leave, regardless of which manager or location handles the request. The Department of Labor requires covered employers to provide specific notices to employees, including notifying them of their eligibility and rights and responsibilities, and formally designating leave as FMLA-qualifying once the employer has enough information to make that determination. (U.S. Department of Labor, Family and Medical Leave Act)


For growing companies, FMLA documentation is really one piece of a larger leave and absence recordkeeping challenge that gets harder as headcount and locations multiply. That broader topic, including how FMLA leave tracking fits into overall employee records and leave management, is covered in Employee Records and Leave Management Software FAQs for Growing Companies.
How does handling FMLA internally differ from getting compliance support
Handling FMLA internally means an owner, controller, or HR generalist is personally responsible for correctly applying employer coverage rules, eligibility calculations, the 12-month measurement method, paid leave substitution policy, benefits continuation, and job restoration standards, consistently, every time a leave request comes in, often alongside a dozen other responsibilities. For a company that has just crossed the 50-employee threshold, this is frequently the first time anyone in the building has had to apply these rules at all.
